Lifelong Learning: Memory vs our Experience Recent works [5, 6, 16, 20] propose maintaining a global memory to store the 3D structure of the environment for embodied tasks, offering a promising solution for life- long navigation. While sharing a similar spirit of evolv- ing decision-making through historical experience, our ap- proach diverges in three key aspects: (1) Dependency: Up- dating such memories typically necessitates computation- ally heavy localization tools (e.g., SLAM [6, 16]) to con- struct explicit representations, whereas our framework is SLAM-free, eliminating the need for complex geometric mapping; (2) Content: Existing methods primarily store raw geometric structures that lack task-specific semantics, while our method enhances policies via task-oriented ex- perience and procedural reasoning; (3) Generalization: Such memory systems are inherently limited to revisiting the same environments, whereas EvoNav generalizes ef- fectively to unseen environments. Overall, by shifting from scene-specific geometry to generalizable semantic and procedural knowledge, our approach offers stronger gener- alization, richer decision reuse, and higher scalability. Recently, with the rapid development of large language models (LLMs) [1, 8, 18, 22], following powerful reason- ing ability and rich commonsense knowledge, LLM-based paradigms have become a promising approach for embod- ied navigation. The emerging works have attempted to extend these versatile LLMs and adapt them for VLN- CE [2, 11, 26, 55, 57], achieving brilliant progress in ad- dressing the drawbacks of poor generalization under the training-based paradigm. As shown in the top right of Fig- ure 1, these works generally use multiple generalist visual translators (e.g., BLIP-2 [28]) to translate visual scenes into universal linguistic text [13, 26] and then reason about nav- igation actions with rich world knowledge in LLMs. Despite the significant progress achieved by LMMs, these methods use extra visual translators to indirectly pro- cess visual environments rather than using LLMs, leading to poor reasoning of visual details. More importantly, these methods simply perform naive reasoning [12, 35, 53] for decision-making and lack the feedback of backtracking his- tory and predicting future, e.g., reviewing errors of histori- cal episodes and imagining potential results of future. Such feedback is more valuable, especially for those failure cases. Therefore, this leads to a question: have we fully unleashed the potential of LLMs for zero-shot VLN-CE? In this paper, the answer is “NO”. The above paradigm relying on naive reasoning without feedback may suffer from heavy decision hallucination for those failed tasks. Consequently, it may encounter continuous failure for those initial navigation error tasks. In contrast, like humans in navigation, we can continuously evolve our decision- making from history to future feedback [7, 25], following history →now →future. Among them, in assisting current decision-making, we summarize historical errors to provide experience while imagining future results to avoid risk. In light of this, it inspires us to follow the human mechanism for evolving agents in navigation. Thus, this paper rethink LLM-based zero-shot VLN-CE and propose a new frame- work, named EvoNav, to improve the agent’s decision- making by history experience and future thought. Specifically, as illustrated at the bottom of Figure 1, EvoNav addresses the above process by two insightful rea- soning: ❶History Chain-of-Experience (H-CoE) and ❷ Future Chain-of-Thought (F-CoT). For ❶H-CoE, it pro- vides history experience from two complementary sources: textual trajectory experience and visual scene experience. Among them, the textual trajectory experience provides global guidance for navigation episodes, while the visual scene experience delivers local visual images for naviga- tion step. For ❷F-CoT, it provides future thought by pre- dicting future actions and landmarks, which assist agent to track the current navigation progress and potential moving directions. The history experience and future thought are cooperative to refine the agent’s decision-making. Both ex- tensive experiments in the simulator and real-world envi- ronment demonstrate the effectiveness of our EvoNav. In summary, our main contributions are: • We rethink LLM-based zero-shot VLN-CE and present a new history-future reasoning paradigm, named EVONAV, which evolves the agent’s decision-making by backtrack- ing history experience and predicting future thought. • We present a Future Chain-of-Thought (F-CoT) rea- soning, which predicts future actions and landmarks as thought to assist the agent in tracking current navigation progress and direction prediction. • We present a History Chain-of-Experience (H-CoE) reasoning, which summarizes textual trajectories and vi- sual scenes from historical episodes as experience to im- prove current decision-making. For thorough examination (§5), we test EVONAV across several diverse open- and closed-source LMMs. Experi- mental results demonstrate that EVONAV outperforms the counterparts, e.g., +20% SR, +21% OSR, and +17% SPL gains over R2R-CE [6], +6% SR, +7% OSR, and +4% SPL on more complex NavRAG-CE [48], which requires agents deeper understanding of user demands. EVONAV not only helps release the reasoning power of existing LLMs, but also evidences the merits of historical experience and future thought methods in challenging VLN-CE decision-making. Vision-and-Language Navigation Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) tasks involve agents navigating to target locations based on natural lan- guage instructions. Traditional approaches primarily used discrete settings with the MP3D simulator [9], where navi- gation was based on predefined graphs and fixed node selec- tions. To enable more realistic interactions, the continuous environment setting (VLN-CE) was introduced, allowing agents to move freely using low-level actions. Initial VLN- CE methods employed encoder-decoder architectures [6] with LSTMs and attention [3, 16, 19, 27, 32, 36, 40– 43, 45, 49–52]. With the rise of vision Transformers [15], adapting Transformer models for VLN-CE became preva- lent [5, 10, 21, 31, 33, 46]. Recent works fine-tuning large models, such as Navid [54] of scaling to 550k samples for training LLM, offer promising solutions. However, training VLN models on domain-specific data limits their zero-shot generalization on unseen environments. This paper focuses on the more challenging and practical setting of zero-shot VLN-CE, aiming to improve LLM-based agents’ decision- making by historical experience and future thought. 15178

Overview framework of EvoNav. EvoNav addresses zero-shot VLN-CE with two complementary reasoning schemes: Future Chain-of-Thought (F-CoT) and History Chain-of-Experience (H-CoE). Given panoramic RGB and depth images, a standard waypoint predictor [20] first identifies candidate waypoint images. These images are then analyzed by the F-CoT, which predicts next-step actions and landmarks as thoughts to guide current navigation progress and direction. After that, H-CoE retrieves trajectory- and scene-related experience from a dynamic experience bank that continuously summarizes and stores completed trajectories and visited scenes. Finally, the retrieved historical experiences and future thoughts are fused within the action prediction module to support decision-making. 2.2. Large Language Models for Navigation With the emergence of large language models (LLMs), recent works have explored their potential in VLN-CE. Some approaches use LLMs as navigation planners, such as DiscussNav [29], A2Nav [13], CA-Nav [12], and Open- Nav [35]. To enhance LLM-based agents with naviga- tion knowledge, some works scale domain-specific data or train additional navigation modules [38, 54, 58]. While these methods improve performance, they hinder sim-to- real transfer in VLN-CE, as they require extra data training. Additionally, these LLM-based works typically perform di- rect unidirectional reasoning for decision-making and lack feedback, they may fail continuously after an initial nav- igation error, resulting in poor decision-making. In con- trast, this paper propose an EvoNav framework for zero- shot VLN-CE that improves the agent’s decision-making by history experience and future thought. 2.3. Lifelong Learning The most recent works [17, 23, 47, 56] propose to main- tain global memory to store environment 3D structure for embodied tasks, offering a promising solution in address- ing embodied navigation with lifelong learning. Such a memory-based approach shares a similar spirit with us in evolving agents’ decision-making with history experience, but differs in key aspects. First, maintaining and updat- ing such memories typically relies on complex localiza- tion tools (e.g., SLAM [23, 47]) to construct environment representation, while our experience is free from these ex- tra tools. Second, these methods primarily directly store geometric structure but lack task-related knowledge, while our experience improves its via task-related experience and thought. Third, such memories are useful only when the agent revisits the same environment, while EvoNav experi- ence can generalize to new environments. 3. Evaluation protocol and GT trajectory To clarify, EvoNav strictly adheres to the training-free zero-shot protocol, utilizing only the agent’s own historical path (H∗) and post-hoc metrics (SR/SPL) rather than sim- ulator ground truth (GT). The “corrected process” is gener- ated via LLM Self-Reflection, where the model critiques its own trajectory against the original instructions to “re- imagine” a more logical navigational sequence. While these imagined paths may not perfectly align with the GT, they function as critical experiences to diagnose reasoning flaws and refine future decision reliability. This experience-driven mechanism simulates human-like reflection on failure with- out external supervision, ensuring a fair comparison with Open-Nav by strictly avoiding training, GT storage, or GT trajectory. 3

Conclusion This paper rethinks LLM-based zero-shot VLN-CE and introduces a framework with the history-future reasoning (named EvoNav) for zero-shot VLN-CE, which improves the agent’s decision-making by history experience and fu- ture thought via Future Chain-of-Thought (F-CoT) and History Chain-of-Experience (H-CoE). F-CoT predicts fu- ture actions and landmarks as thoughts to assist navigation progress estimation and direction selection, while H-CoE summarizes historical trajectories and scenes as experience to improve navigation decision reliability. In future work, we aim to explore the multi-agent collaboration to improve the reasoning ability of LLM-based agents.
